chef_bio.origin: Downtown Kyoto (Nakagyo), a short walk from Shijo Kawaramachi
chef_bio.background: VOG is Kyoto's all-in-one vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free Indian kitchen, where the name itself spells out the mission: Vegetarian & Vegan, Organic, Gluten-free. The whole menu is meat-free and egg-free, built around Kyo Yasai, the heirloom vegetables that Kyoto farmers have cultivated for centuries. The owner is very much the heart of the place: he is multilingual, switching between English, Japanese and another Asian language, and he likes to come to the table to walk diners through the food himself, so even people new to vegan eating feel looked after. Guests often mention ending up in long conversations with him about his life and his family, which gives the small dining room a warm, personal feel. Dishes are served on hand-crafted local ceramics, Kyo-yaki, Kiyomizu-yaki and Shigaraki-yaki, and a complimentary soup arrives in a traditional wooden kuksa cup.
chef_bio.philosophy: A nourishing, plant-based approach the kitchen sums up with its 'No White Food' campaign: brown rice, whole-grain and gluten-free flours, and natural, unprocessed ingredients over refined white ones, leaning on Kyoto's seasonal heirloom vegetables for flavor.
chef_bio.specialty: Plant-based Indian cooking made entirely vegetarian and vegan, with a wide range of dishes that can also be prepared gluten-free or Jain. Diners single out the spinach (palak) curry and dal, garlic naan, samosas, paneer-style butter masala, the vegan roll cake, and the salted lassi.

anecdotes.text: Diners describe the multilingual owner personally explaining the dishes, so even those unfamiliar with vegan food feel reassured, and several mention having heartfelt conversations with him about his life and family.
The restaurant frames its mission around the 'No White Food' idea and Kyoto's heritage Kyo Yasai vegetables, serving food on local Kyo-yaki, Kiyomizu-yaki and Shigaraki-yaki ceramics.

gf_cross_contamination.text: VOG is a fully gluten-free-oriented kitchen that uses whole-grain and gluten-free flours, and gluten-free items are labeled on the menu. No source documents a specific cross-contamination protocol or a dedicated fryer, so celiacs should confirm prep separation directly with the owner, who is hands-on and explains dishes personally.
gf_cross_contamination.why: ALARMING for a celiac. The cited site never calls the kitchen gluten-free-oriented, and its own navigation carries a whole menu section 'Rice, Naan & Roti -> Rice | Naans | Rotis'. Naan and roti are wheat, tandoor-baked in the same kitchen, and dozens of HappyCow reviews rave about the garlic naan.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No source confirms whether any soy-based sauces used (for example in the 'butter soy meat' style curry) are wheat-free. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so a strict celiac should verify the specific sauce with staff.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire kitchen is vegetarian with no meat, fish or egg on the menu, which removes the usual animal cross-contact risks for vegans.
vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: 'We are an authentic vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, and Jain-friendly restaurant in Kyoto. All our main dishes are freshly cooked to order and can be adjusted for spice level.' ChIJVc1NH3sJAWAR9SMlbODV9NQ.notes: The rare fully GF + vegan ramen in Japan. Soy-milk broth, rice-flour noodles, GF gyoza & cakes. Gion. Walk-in; expect a queue.

chef_bio.background: Gion Soy Milk Ramen was founded by Uno Yukiko, a Kyoto-born pastry chef and plant-based cuisine researcher who began her career as a chef before moving into pastry. Her path toward ramen started with people, not recipes: working with customers who had food allergies, she developed a cake made entirely from plant-based ingredients with no wheat, dairy, or eggs. A pivotal moment came when she met a boy with 23 allergies, and she spent years thinking about how to let people who are limited in what they can eat finally enjoy a bowl of ramen. She opened the Gion shop on October 12, 2022. It is an intimate counter restaurant near Gion-Shijo Station where the entire kitchen is built to be free of gluten and animal products. Uno also runs a plant-based sweets shop, Mushiyashanai, in Ichijoji.
chef_bio.philosophy: Uno's stated mission is to remove food barriers and deliver deliciousness to everyone, making all people smile with food. She has described the ramen as gentle enough to be eaten by babies who have finished weaning, and says the moments when allergic families tell her they can finally feel safe eating somewhere reaffirm why she does this work.
chef_bio.specialty: The house bowl is the Soy Milk Ramen 'Yuki' (Snow): a creamy broth built from her own house-made soy milk together with vegetables, mushrooms and kelp, seasoned with gluten-free soy sauce. The noodles are an original recipe made from rice flour kneaded with kelp, giving them a distinctive smooth, slippery texture. The kitchen also offers a spicy soy-milk dan dan noodle bowl and bowls piled with a wide range of Japanese vegetables. Diners are encouraged to finish with rice to turn the remaining broth into a risotto.

anecdotes.text: Uno traces the whole project to one encounter: 'It all started when I met a boy with 23 allergies. For about four years now, I've been thinking that I want people who are limited in what they can eat to enjoy ramen.'

Before opening the ramen shop she developed a fully plant-based cake with no wheat, dairy or eggs; an encounter with a British vegan traveler who loved it helped inspire her broader mission to create dining experiences that matter to people who are usually left out.

The signature 'Yuki' bowl pairs her house-made soy milk broth with original rice-flour-and-kelp noodles seasoned with gluten-free soy sauce, and the shop says the bowl is gentle enough for babies who have finished weaning.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site (soymilkramen.com / en.soymilkramen.com) tells the founding story of pastry chef Uno Yukiko: a 100% plant-based 'miracle cake' with no wheat/dairy/eggs, a British vegan traveler who loved it, the mission 'to make all people smile with food', and ramen safe from babies who have finished weaning. Leaf Kyoto confirms the boy with 23 allergies, the ~four-year gestation, the Oct 12 2022 opening near Gion-Shijo, the 1,500 yen 'Snow' bowl, and the Mushiyashanai sweets shop in Ichijoji.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a dedicated gluten-free and plant-based kitchen: the restaurant states all menu items are gluten-free and plant-based, the kitchen contains no gluten or animal products, and customers are asked not to bring those items into the dining area. Because there is no wheat in the kitchen at all, the usual ramen cross-contamination risks (shared noodle water, shared broth) are largely removed.
A celiac-conscious diner highlighted the advantage of an all-gluten-free operation, noting 'not having to worry about cross contamination when it comes to soup especially.'
gf_cross_contamination.why: ALARMING MISATTRIBUTION. The quote is verbatim and on the right venue's listing, but the reviewer is a VEGAN talking about ANIMAL cross-contact — their own parenthesis says they stopped eating at meat restaurants after finding chicken in their soup. Nothing marks them as celiac or gluten-conscious.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The noodles themselves are gluten-free, made from rice flour kneaded with kelp rather than wheat; reviewers describe them as smooth and slightly spaghetti-like.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Unlike most Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, this restaurant specifically uses gluten-free soy sauce in its broth and seasoning, so the soup is described as gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The entire operation is vegan with no animal products in the kitchen, which removes the typical risk of vegan cross-contact from shared meat or dashi-based broths found in conventional ramen shops.
Tabelog reviews describe it as a completely vegan ramen shop where all menu items are plant-based.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Reviewers praise the allergen transparency, noting items are 'very clearly labeled for all kinds of allergens, such as soy, gluten and wheat.'

The restaurant says it can accommodate other specific allergies on request and offers nut-free and mushroom-free options. Given the soy milk broth, soy-allergic diners should confirm options directly, as the menu is soy-forward.

positives.text: A genuinely dedicated gluten-free and vegan kitchen founded specifically to serve people with allergies and dietary restrictions, which is rare for ramen and unusually safe for celiac diners compared to typical wheat-and-dashi ramen shops.
Gluten-free soy sauce and rice-flour noodles mean the broth and noodles are both made without wheat.
Reviewers report clear allergen labeling and a celiac diner specifically noted not having to worry about cross-contamination in the soup.
positives.why: Second half repeats the misattribution: nobody on this listing identifies as celiac, and the cross-contamination remark is explicitly about meat in soup. The allergen-labelling half is fine. Split the claim and drop the 'celiac diner' assertion.

chef_bio.background: CHOICE was founded by a doctor — a plastic surgeon and cosmetic dermatologist with decades of experience who helped pioneer laser and aesthetic medicine in Japan. The turning point came after March 2011, when concerns about the safety and quality of food set the founder on a path of studying nutrition seriously. That study hardened into a simple conviction: you are what you eat, and many skin and health problems trace back to the plate rather than the symptom. CHOICE grew out of that belief — a whole-foods, plant-based cafe near Sanjo where the entire menu is built to be both gluten-free and vegan, made from organic, natural, unprocessed ingredients.
chef_bio.philosophy: The founder's guiding idea is that treating a symptom is not the same as curing its cause, and that genuine health starts with what you eat. Just as important is the belief that food should be enjoyed — eating with joy, in their words, helps the body digest and absorb nutrition properly — so the cooking aims to be satisfying and delicious, not merely virtuous. The whole-foods, plant-based approach is framed as good for both personal health and the planet.
chef_bio.specialty: CHOICE is known for being one of Kyoto's go-to spots where vegans, vegetarians and gluten-free eaters can order anything on the menu without worry. Standouts include crisp gluten-free pizzas, pancakes, and two corn-penne pastas: a tomato-sauce version topped with house-made vegan mozzarella, and a pesto penne built on a vibrant spinach-and-chlorella sauce. The kitchen leans on its own fermented vegan cheeses, brown rice, and an array of cakes and sweets, with coffee and pancakes as everyday favorites.

anecdotes.text: The cafe traces its origin to 2011, when worries about food safety led the founder — a longtime plastic surgeon and cosmetic dermatologist — to immerse themselves in the study of food and nutrition, eventually opening CHOICE around the conviction that 'you are what you eat.'

Both of the pasta dishes are made with 100% corn penne — a tomato-sauce penne with homemade vegan mozzarella, and a pesto penne with a spinach-and-chlorella sauce — so even the pasta stays gluten-free and vegan.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hs-choice.com's founder message states the founder is a plastic surgeon/cosmetic dermatologist of 30+ years who pioneered laser surgery and 'medical esthetic' treatment in Japan, and after the March 11 2011 disaster turned to studying food and nutrition ('you are what you eat'; 'eating with joy makes food digested and absorbed well'). The meal page states dishes are gluten-free and vegan and that both pastas use 100% corn penne.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The entire establishment is 100% gluten-free: the kitchen states it uses no wheat, barley, oats or rye anywhere on the menu. Because no gluten-containing ingredients are present in the building, the usual sources of cross-contamination are largely removed — though the venue is not explicitly described as a certified celiac-dedicated facility, so those with severe celiac disease may wish to confirm prep details directly.
gf_cross_contamination.why: ALARM — the biggest defect on this shard. The cited page carries an explicit wheat exception, and ancient wheat contains gluten. The 'no wheat, barley, oats or rye' sentence the claim quotes is real but lives on the co-cited Tabelog listing ('Our café is completely free of animal products… We also d

gf_cross_contamination.text: Every dish is gluten-free and vegan, including the two pasta dishes, which are made with 100% corn penne rather than wheat pasta.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: CHOICE uses tamari shoyu (gluten-free soy sauce) in its cooking instead of standard wheat-based soy sauce, and the soup broth is made without fish flakes.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is entirely plant-based — no meat, fish, eggs, dairy or honey are used anywhere on the menu — so vegan cross-contact risk is inherently minimal since no animal products are present in the kitchen at all.

staff_allergy_handling.text: A reviewer noted that staff were very helpful with allergy information and that English is spoken, making it easier to confirm dietary needs.

positives.text: Widely recommended as one of the best places in Kyoto for vegans, vegetarians and gluten-free eaters, where the whole menu is safe to order from.
positives.why: ALARM: the first clause is verbatim, but 'the whole menu is safe to order from' is contradicted by the very next sentence on the cited page, which carves out the pasta dishes. Delete that clause — it is exactly the sort of line that stops a celiac asking.

positives.text: A diner summed it up simply: 'Everything is gluten-free!' — the entire menu is both gluten-free and vegan.

chef_bio.background: cafe planet opened in November 2021 on the banks of the Kamogawa River, just a short walk from the Kamo Delta where the Takano and Kamo rivers meet. It is a bright, simple and modern riverside space with an indoor terrace and river-facing seating. The cafe is the sister establishment of CHOICE, an established gluten-free and vegan cafe in Kyoto, and carries the same plant-based philosophy to this Kamogawa-side location. It is also openly dog-friendly, a direction shaped by the owner's own love of dogs, with hours suited to dog walks and even plant-based dog treats and latte art featuring a pet's face.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cafe is built on the idea that plant-based, healthy eating should be genuinely delicious -- summed up in its own words as 'Vegan is delicious!' The whole menu is vegan and gluten-free, using organic, additive-free ingredients chosen with care for their origin and production method.
chef_bio.specialty: Known for a fully vegan and gluten-free menu where every item avoids dairy, eggs, and wheat. The signature is a gluten-free pizza built on a rice-flour crust described as chewy right to the edge, topped with a vegan cheese made from fermented cashew nuts and seasonal vegetables on a tomato base. Other favorites include acai bowls, vegetable-packed tomato-based chilled pasta made with corn penne, fresh seasonal salads, and house desserts such as chocolate terrine and pound cake.

chef_bio.background: Cafe Vegan Terrace (also listed as Cafe Tea Terrace) is a small, calm vegan cafe tucked inside the Gion Elite Terrace hotel in Kyoto's Higashiyama / Gion district. Set just off the busy streets, it serves a fully plant-based menu to hotel guests and walk-in diners alike, and is known as a quiet retreat for an unhurried lunch in the heart of historic Gion.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cooking follows the principles of shojin ryori (Buddhist temple cuisine): dishes are built entirely from plants and deliberately exclude the five pungent alliums (onion, garlic, leek, chives, shallots), so the menu also suits diners avoiding those ingredients for religious reasons. Much of the menu is gluten-free, with gluten-free options offered for the sandwich and burger.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan ramen is the standout: a surprisingly rich, savory broth built without garlic, leeks, onions, or chives, served with millet noodles that hold their texture better than rice noodles. The kitchen also turns out soy-sauce and yuba-yuzu ramen, a teriyaki soy-meat burger, turmeric-yellow vegetable curry, and sweets like matcha pudding and dango.

anecdotes.text: A diner who tried the ramen called it one of their favorites in Kyoto, noting the broth was 'super flavorful, which was a surprise because it was made without garlic, leeks, onions, or chives to follow the principles of Shojin Ryori,' and that the kitchen uses millet noodles for better texture.

Reviewers describe it as a 'cute cafe away from the hustle and bustle of nearby streets,' a calm and cosy spot attached to a hotel with very friendly staff, and note a gluten-free sandwich and a burger on gluten-free bread are available on request.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The cafe advertises a vegan and gluten-free menu, with most dishes gluten-free and gluten-free options offered for the sandwich and burger. Celiac and wheat-allergic diners should ask specifically whether the soy sauce used in the ramen and teriyaki burger is wheat-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is fully vegan, so there is no animal-product cross-contact to worry about; the entire menu is plant-based.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The cafe takes reservations (reportedly in advance) and can accommodate special dietary requests, including avoiding particular ingredients for religious reasons. Diners are advised to flag ingredients to avoid when booking.

chef_bio.background: Tucked just off the tourist bustle of Arashiyama, near Hankyu Arashiyama Station, Musubi began with a simple idea built into its name: musubi, the act of connecting people to one another. The cafe pairs a relaxed, homely space (including a tatami room that families love) with a mission of being "kind to heart and body." Unusually for a cafe, it was set up with active travelers in mind too, offering showers and lockers so that runners, hikers, and climbers exploring the hills and river around Arashiyama have a welcoming place to refuel. Its sister operation, Musubi Sweets Factory, grew out of a wish that people who normally cannot eat cake, those with egg, dairy, or wheat allergies, and especially children, could finally sit down with family and friends and enjoy dessert too.
chef_bio.philosophy: Food should be gentle on both mind and body, made with locally sourced ingredients, and shared in a way that connects people: "when people connect, happiness spreads." The team also believes no one should be left out of a treat, building a dessert program specifically so allergy sufferers and children can enjoy cake alongside everyone else.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegetable-forward, health-conscious cooking served as lunch and dinner sets, with daily blackboard specials where one option is always vegan-friendly. Signature savory plates include chickpea and tomato curry, butternut squash and Manganji pepper keema curry, taco rice, and vegetable pasta. The cafe is best known, though, for its desserts: a lineup of sweets that are 100% vegan and gluten-free, including a musubi parfait and butter-style sandwich, made so that those with egg, dairy, or wheat allergies can enjoy them.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen is known for going out of its way for guests: one visitor recalled the staff being incredibly friendly and still preparing them a vegan lunch set even though it had technically sold out for the day.

Beyond a meal, the cafe doubles as a base for active travelers, with shower booths and lockers (day-use around 500 yen) so runners, hikers, and climbers can clean up and refuel after exploring Arashiyama.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site (musubi-cafe.jp) frames the name around 'when people connect, HAPPY chains onward', the tagline 'kind to heart and body', and describes Musubi Sweets Factory's 100% vegan & gluten-free sweets for those with egg/dairy/wheat allergies. The service page confirms shower booths, fitting rooms and lockers (about 500 yen day-use) supporting runners and hikers based near the Togetsukyo Bridge.

chef_bio.background: stope. is a small, fully plant-based cafe tucked near Nijo Castle, run as a family affair by a husband-and-wife team who often have their young daughter around. Before opening their own place, the owner cooked at Ain Soph, one of Japan's best-known vegan restaurant groups, and that pedigree shows up in the cooking. The result is a warm, low-key neighborhood spot where regulars and travelers alike are greeted personally and the kitchen is happy to tweak dishes or whip up an off-menu drink on request.
chef_bio.philosophy: 100% plant-based cooking served in a relaxed, family-run setting, with friendly, accommodating service.
chef_bio.specialty: An all-vegan menu spanning comfort-food savories and indulgent desserts: a much-praised vegan cheeseburger (grilled onion, avocado, lettuce, tomato), a rich 'milky' black-garlic ramen, a teriyaki Buddha bowl, Japanese curry, and minestrone soup, followed by parfaits, gateau chocolat, and big vegan sundaes. Many dishes can also be made gluten-free.

anecdotes.text: Diners describe it as a cute spot run by a friendly husband and wife who have a darling little daughter, with a chill, welcoming atmosphere.
Regulars note the owner previously worked at Ain Soph, a well-known vegan restaurant, before opening stope.

gf_cross_contamination.text: stope. is a fully vegan kitchen, but it is a small shared kitchen rather than a dedicated gluten-free facility. chef_bio.background: Towzen began in 2004, when Minoru Yonekawa opened a small ramen shop near Shimogamo Shrine in northern Kyoto. The Yonekawa family had deep roots in tofu-making, and that heritage led to a single, defining experiment: building a ramen broth not on pork or chicken bones, but on soy milk. That creamy soy-milk base became the soul of the shop. Towzen bills itself as the shop that developed the first vegan ramen in Japan, and over two decades it has grown into one of the country's longest-running and most celebrated vegan ramen establishments. Tucked into a house in the quiet suburbs north of the city, it has built a devoted following and even taken its bowls beyond Kyoto, to kitchens as far as Kuala Lumpur, Batam and Sydney.
chef_bio.philosophy: Yonekawa calls his concept 'World Peace Ramen' — exceptional flavor married with compassion and cultural integrity. The cooking draws on Buddhist shojin ryori (temple cuisine), prepared without animal products or alliums, intended as nourishment for both body and spirit.
chef_bio.specialty: Soy-milk ramen built on a 100% organic soy-milk broth. The signature 'Musashi' bowl is a creamy, velvety soy-milk broth flavored with kelp and soy sauce, dusted with sansho pepper and topped with slices of yuba, simmered mushrooms, and a dab of tart plum paste. The 'tantanmen' uses the same broth swirled with chili paste and savory simmered soy-bean 'meat' — spicy and rich without being heavy.

anecdotes.text: The whole restaurant grew out of one experiment rooted in the Yonekawa family's tofu tradition: replacing the usual meat-bone ramen broth with soy milk. That creamy soy-milk base is what makes the bowl so distinctively rich.
Towzen describes itself as the original vegan ramen shop, having developed and served what it calls the first vegan ramen in Japan — operating since July 2004.

The Musashi bowl pairs a kelp-and-soy-sauce-flavored soy-milk broth with sansho pepper, yuba, simmered mushrooms and a dab of plum paste; the tantanmen swirls in chili paste and simmered soy-bean meat.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog lists the opening day as 2004.7.26 and quotes the shop calling itself the original vegan ramen shop that 'developed and invented the first vegan Ramen in Japan, and in fact the world', using 100% organic soy milk in a tonkotsu-style soy-milk broth. towzenramen.com confirms founder Minoru Yonekawa, the family tofu tradition, 'World Peace Ramen', shojin-style no-animal/no-allium cooking, and branches in Kyoto, Kuala Lumpur, Batam and Sydney.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Gluten-free rice noodles are available as a substitute for the standard wheat ramen noodles (some noodle swaps carry a small fee). One reviewer specifically described ordering 'tantan ramen with soy meat and rice noodles (gluten free noodles).'
The shop also notes gluten-free options on its menu and offers gluten-free cakes, indicating real awareness of gluten-free diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Unlike most ramen shops, Towzen states it uses gluten-free soy sauce, which it boils down (along with mirin) to reduce alcohol content below 0.1%. This addresses the usual wheat-in-soy-sauce concern that makes most ramen broths unsafe for celiacs.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen has been fully vegan (100% plant-based) since 2018, with broth built on organic soy milk rather than meat or fish stock — so there is no cross-contact with animal products.
The cooking follows shōjin ryōri principles, prepared without animal products or alliums (onion/garlic), which also makes it suitable for stricter Buddhist and oriental-vegan diners.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Orders are highly customizable — diners can choose flavor, spice level, portion size and noodle type, and reviewers note staff speak good English, making it easier to communicate dietary needs.
The menu lists oriental-vegan, halal and gluten-free options, showing the staff routinely accommodate dietary requests.

positives.text: Fully vegan kitchen with no animal-product cross-contact — a rare confident choice for plant-based diners.

Genuine gluten-free pathway: gluten-free rice noodles plus gluten-free soy sauce, which is unusual for a ramen shop. Celiac diners should still confirm noodle-boiling and shared-equipment handling in person.

chef_bio.background: Maru is a fully gluten-free cafe and bar tucked away on the third floor of a building in Kiyamachi, one of Kyoto's liveliest streets near Shijo-Kawaramachi. The owner opened it after developing a wheat allergy about ten years ago, having suffered sudden, full-body hives. Wishing there were an accessible, welcoming place to eat well without wheat, she created exactly that: a kitchen where no wheat products are handled at all, and where even bringing wheat-containing items into the premises is not allowed. The head chef is Japanese and follows a gluten-free diet herself, and she leans on Kyoto ingredients wherever possible, seasoning with fermented staples like salt koji and rice miso rather than reaching for wheat-based shortcuts.
chef_bio.philosophy: That eating without wheat should be easy, delicious, and unremarkable. By keeping the entire kitchen and room free of wheat, the owner offers people with wheat allergies and celiac disease a place where they can relax and simply enjoy a meal or a drink.
chef_bio.specialty: An all-gluten-free menu where wheat flour is swapped for rice flour throughout. Diners single out the gluten-free fried chicken, the curry, vegan-friendly stews and grilled vegetables, soy milk ice cream, and a full bar of carefully chosen gluten-free drinks and cocktails. The kitchen seasons with salt koji, rice miso, and gluten-free soy sauce.

anecdotes.text: The owner developed a wheat allergy roughly ten years ago after a sudden bout of full-body hives, and opened Maru because she wished there were an accessible place to eat well without wheat nearby. No wheat products are handled in the kitchen, and wheat items are not allowed onto the premises at all.

The head chef is Japanese and follows a gluten-free diet herself; the kitchen uses Kyoto ingredients where possible, seasoned with salt koji, rice miso, and gluten-free soy sauce, and the whole menu, including bar-time dishes, is gluten-free.
Diners highlight the gluten-free fried chicken, curry, and even gluten-free cocktails, noting the bar is 'a hidden gluten-free' spot near Shijo-Kawaramachi.

The owner cautions that, because trace wheat contamination during the manufacturing of Japanese ingredients cannot be completely ruled out, those with severe wheat allergy should refrain (重度の方はお控えくださいませ). Highly sensitive celiac diners should weigh this and confirm directly.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The kitchen uses gluten-free soy sauce rather than standard wheat-based soy sauce, and seasons with fermented staples like salt koji and rice miso.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegan options exist but are limited; the place is gluten-free first, and most of the menu contains animal products. Reviewers report vegan versions of curry and white stew, plus salad, soup, grilled vegetables, and soy milk ice cream.

The owner openly advises that severe wheat-allergy cases should refrain, showing transparency about the limits of what a no-wheat-on-premises kitchen can guarantee.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, Japan — near the Philosopher's Path, a short walk from Ginkakuji (the Silver Pavilion)
chef_bio.background: Kuru Kuru is a tiny, warmly personal cafe tucked along the route to Ginkakuji, run single-handedly by a woman who is gluten-intolerant herself. Because she cannot eat gluten, she built the whole place around that need: every single item on the menu is gluten-free, made by her own hands. The room is small and homey, and regulars describe the whole project as a genuine labor of love. Because she runs it alone, there can be a short wait at busy times — part of the charm of a place where one person is cooking, baking and serving everything.
chef_bio.philosophy: Everything is gluten-free, made from scratch by the owner so that someone who shares her intolerance can eat the entire menu without worry — hospitality grounded in her own lived experience.
chef_bio.specialty: She is best known for her cakes — light, airy chiffon and rice-flour cakes in a rotating range of flavors (around four at a time) that diners single out as the highlight. On the savory side she makes a rice-flour pizza and a vegan chickpea curry, and the menu also includes gluten-free spaghetti. Drinks lean refreshing and homemade, including a plum soda, matcha, and ginger, lemon and rooibos teas.

anecdotes.text: Reviewers describe the owner as a lovely, very kind and helpful woman who runs the tiny cafe largely on her own, and who has been known to surprise guests with complimentary treats — and to offer samples when a customer mentions they also eat gluten-free.
Visitors call it a nice discovery on the walk toward Ginkakuji, singling out that the curry and pizza are great and describing the owner as 'so lovely.'
Several diners note that the rice-flour pizza won over even the gluten-eaters in their group, with one calling it the best gluten-free crust they had had.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The entire menu is gluten-free because the owner is gluten-intolerant herself, which removes wheat-flour from the core of the kitchen and is the biggest single point in the cafe's favor for GF diners.

Celiac diners should confirm preparation directly with the owner.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: At least one reviewer warns that the bento box is not safe for celiacs because it contains soy sauce — a reminder that standard Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat. Ask which items use soy sauce before ordering.

vegan_cross_contact.text: There are dedicated vegan options, notably a vegan chickpea curry, and reviewers mention plenty of vegan items; no specific reports were found on vegan cross-contact in a kitchen that also handles dairy cakes and cheese, so vegan diners should confirm shared-equipment handling with the owner.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The cafe is run by a single owner who is gluten-intolerant herself and is described as kind and helpful, which makes direct conversation about your needs straightforward — but it also means there is no separate trained allergy team, so clear, item-by-item questions are worthwhile.

positives.text: Everything on the menu is gluten-free, made from scratch by an owner who shares the intolerance — rare and reassuring for GF diners.

chef_bio.background: waco crepes is a tiny, six-seat creperie tucked into Miyagawa-cho, one of Kyoto's historic geisha quarters in the Higashiyama district, where you can still cross paths with maiko and geiko on the lanes outside. The shop set out to do something unusual: make every single item gluten-free and vegan without it feeling like a compromise. The crepes are built on an original fermented rice-flour batter using house-blended organic rice flour, organic soy milk, and organic apples and vegetables, which gives them their distinctive mochi-like chew with crisp edges. Each batter is mixed fresh and each crepe griddled individually to order. The standout is a handmade soy whipped cream made from tofu and vanilla bean, and the kitchen leans on dairy-free cheese and chocolate alternatives so the roughly fifty menu options stay fully plant-based. Despite its six-seat footprint, the shop has built a devoted following among celiac and vegan travelers, and sells its own original merchandise such as tenugui hand towels and eco-bags.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cooking that is gentle on the body: a wholly plant-based, gluten-free menu built on organic ingredients, with each crepe batter mixed and griddled to order.
chef_bio.specialty: Fermented rice-flour crepes (mochi-textured, crisp at the edges) that are entirely gluten-free and plant-based, finished with a signature handmade soy whipped cream made from tofu and vanilla bean. Around 50 sweet and savory variations, from matcha and azuki to avocado-and-vegan-cheese and a much-loved smoked-salmon-style filling.

anecdotes.text: Staff often draw cute little hand-drawn messages on the crepe wrapping paper, a small touch reviewers love.

chef_bio.background: Koma Gallery Cafe is run by the arts organization NPO Koma (NPO高麗), founded by the artist, photographer and writer Keiko Koma (高麗恵子), who established the organization after her parents' deaths and is reported to have funded it from her inheritance, gathering roughly 100 volunteers. Keiko Koma works alongside the musician Idaki Shin (いだきしん, whose real name is reported as Saito Tadamitsu), and the cafe operates as a combined art gallery, cafe and cultural-event space rather than a conventional restaurant — a first-floor cafe where you can hear Idaki Shin's music and a second-floor gallery of Koma's work. Japanese portal material ties the cafe to Koma's cultural projects such as her Goguryeo ('Koma') legends writing and concert work. The cafe is noted for coffee the NPO brings in from Africa (Ethiopia and Tanzania), and Koma has written about 'messages' from African nature and coffee. It is a dedicated gluten-free cafe, serving gluten-free cakes, and looks out on a quiet garden with a view toward the Yasaka Pagoda.
chef_bio.philosophy: Art, coffee and cultural exchange as a path toward a society where people can live in true peace and happiness; the cafe doubles as a gallery and event venue expressing Keiko Koma and Idaki Shin's artistic activities.
chef_bio.specialty: A dedicated gluten-free cafe: gluten-free cakes and sweets (chiffon, matcha and other seasonal cakes, some also dairy-free) and coffee (beans sourced from Africa — Ethiopia and Tanzania — via the NPO), served in a gallery setting with a garden view of the Yasaka Pagoda.

chef_bio.background: AL CAMINO is part of chef Watanabe Takesho's il Viale family of Italian restaurants in Kyoto. His path to cooking began almost by accident: at 21 he traveled to Italy hoping to see Ferraris and Ducati motorcycles, but it was the food that captured him, and he came home determined to cook it. After training at Italian kitchens in Kyoto and Tokyo, he opened his first restaurant, Cucina il Viale, in 1999, and a stint working on a farm in Kyoto's Kamigamo district turned him into a devotee of organic and heirloom Kyoto vegetables. He opened Pizzeria AL CAMINO in 2008, serving wood-fired pizza made with all-Italian ingredients for well over a decade. More recently he reinvented the space entirely, retiring the pizza oven and relaunching AL CAMINO as a gluten-free specialty deli built around rice-flour bread.
chef_bio.philosophy: A conviction that good food wins people over on its own terms. When early diners balked at vegetable-forward plates, Watanabe held the line on the belief that truly delicious things are eventually recognized, the same patient approach he brought to rebuilding AL CAMINO entirely around gluten-free cooking.
chef_bio.specialty: Rice-flour bread panini are the heart of the menu, led by their signature panino, alongside versions like Parma prosciutto and caprese. The kitchen rounds things out with Italian small plates, rice-flour-and-olive-oil chocolate cake and other rice-flour desserts, Italian cookies, fresh-squeezed orange juice, Italian wines, and even a gluten-free Italian beer.

chef_bio.background: SINLESS CAFÉ / Sinless Lab grew out of founder Hisae Sakamoto's years living and working in the food world in Singapore, a country known for its health-forward approach to eating. There, Sakamoto became a researcher of low-sugar cooking and went on to lecture on the subject. The café in central Kyoto is the expression of that research: a 100% gluten-free, sugar-conscious place where the healthier version is the whole point rather than an afterthought. The kitchen leans into ingredients suited to the body, including distinctly Kyoto touches like cakes made with sake lees from the city's Sasaki Sake Brewery.
chef_bio.philosophy: The guiding idea is sweets you can enjoy without the guilt or the after-effects: 'regulating the body with sweets.' Sweetness is coaxed from plant-based ingredients rather than refined sugar, so a full afternoon tea spread carries only about the sugar of a single rice ball and stays easy on the stomach.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the canelé, reworked the Sinless way: made with rice flour instead of wheat and without white sugar, with the rice flour's amount and distribution carefully calibrated to keep a mellow, rich flavor while holding the sugar down. A boxed set of five low-sugar, gluten-free canelés is the most popular thing they make. Beyond the canelé, expect creative sweets, breads, cakes, puddings, cookies, and a reservation-based afternoon tea set built around bite-sized sweets and a Victoria cake.

chef_bio.background: Toshoan grows out of one of Kyoto's old anko houses: a sweet red-bean-paste maker established in 1950, rooted in the city's traditional confectionery trade. In 2012 that bean-paste heritage was reimagined as a modern shop and little cafe a short walk south of Nijo Castle along Horikawa Street, with a refreshed reopening in 2018. The idea is simple but unusual: take the family's craft of making fine 'nama-an' (fresh, smooth red bean paste) and build an entire menu of sweets around it without using any wheat flour at all. The result is a rare thing in Japan, a place where every cake, cookie and pancake is made gluten-free from the ground up rather than as a special-request substitute.
chef_bio.philosophy: Showcasing the craft of fresh red bean paste, and proving that anko-based wagashi can be made entirely without wheat flour so that gluten-free guests can enjoy classic Japanese sweets.
chef_bio.specialty: Gluten-free sweets built on freshly made red bean paste. The cafe is best known for its fluffy gluten-free souffle pancakes, made to order (they take about 30 minutes) and often served with anko and salty butter. The shop side is known for its anko-forward treats: An de Cookies, the An de cheesecake (cream cheese folded with fresh red bean paste), Yokan for Coffee designed to pair with a cup of coffee, sakura anmitsu, and the Miyako Monaka wafer sandwich.

anecdotes.text: The whole shop is wheat-flour-free, with the souffle pancakes as the standout. They are made to order and take about half an hour, but visitors describe them as well worth the wait and a chance to try Japan's famous fluffy pancakes in a gluten-free form.

Toshoan grew from a bean-paste manufacturer founded in 1950; the cafe opened in 2012 and was renewed in 2018, and specializes in treats made from fresh 'nama-an' red bean paste such as An de Cookies, An de cheesecake and Yokan for Coffee.
The matcha souffle pancake in particular is singled out by gluten-free travelers as unforgettable.

chef_bio.background: ZIRAEL is the work of Anna, a Russian founder who opened this tiny plant-based spot in September 2022 in a quiet alley near Yasaka Shrine in Gion. She had been living a vegan lifestyle since 2006 and spent several years in Japan before settling in Kyoto, drawn by the natural surroundings she discovered while traveling the country. She built ZIRAEL around the produce she fell in love with here, sourcing vegetables from growers across the region — Ohara, Tango, Kyotamba, and Kameoka among them. The room seats only a handful of guests, and the warm, personal welcome from the owners is something diners mention again and again.
chef_bio.philosophy: Anna wanted to make plant-based eating in Kyoto effortless for international visitors, who can struggle with Japanese-only labeling elsewhere. As she put it, she would love for foreigners to feel at home here — a place to enjoy a fully plant-based meal without worry. The cooking is 100% plant-based and built first and foremost around showcasing local vegetables.
chef_bio.specialty: Kyoto-vegetable plates are the heart of the menu, with a daily salad that regulars call some of the best they have had, alongside generous mains like soy hamburg steak, ginger-fried soy meat, and vegan dumplings that travelers single out as standouts. The kitchen also reaches back to Anna's roots with dishes such as Ukrainian borscht and a lentil-tomato stew. The plates change day to day with the season and what the farms send, and popular dishes can sell out, so the menu is never quite the same twice.

chef_bio.background: AIN SOPH. Journey Kyoto is the Kansai outpost of the AIN SOPH. group, the all-vegan restaurant family founded by Yuki Shirai, who opened the first AIN SOPH. in Tokyo in 2009 and has been a driving force in Japan's plant-based dining scene ever since. Shirai grew up between two faiths and worldviews: her father's family followed Shingon esoteric Buddhism while her mother's family was Catholic, an upbringing she credits with teaching her to respect and live close to nature. A homestay with a vegan family in Canada introduced her to plant-based living firsthand, and those encounters set her on the path to building AIN SOPH. The Kyoto branch sits on a quiet backstreet just off bustling Kawaramachi, in a building with deep local roots: it formerly housed the Maruni food hall and still honors a guardian tanuki spirit, 'Shichibe-san,' enshrined on site and tied to the nearby Nishiki Tenmangu shrine. The result is a cozy, fully plant-based cafe where Tokyo classics meet Kyoto-only creations.
chef_bio.philosophy: For Shirai, food is a way to reconnect people with nature and with their truest selves. The name 'Ain Soph' is Hebrew for the infinite, which she encountered during a spiritual experience and felt drawn to; her company name, the single character 'Shin' meaning 'truth,' reflects a commitment she draws from tea ceremony to 'not lying to myself and living in truth.' Everything is 100% plant-based - no meat, fish, dairy, eggs or honey - and she frames veganism not as a mandate but as a cuisine that deserves a place alongside Italian, French and Japanese cooking.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan comfort food and 'junk food done right' - the kitchen is known for hearty plant-based burgers, including a Ripple cheese burger and a cutlet (katsu) burger, plus convincing vegan kara-age (fried 'chicken'), onion rings and curries. On the sweet side they serve the group's signature Heavenly vegan pancakes and a Kyoto-original gluten-free matcha pancake, along with seasonal parfaits and vegan brownies and ice cream.

anecdotes.text: Founder Yuki Shirai grew up between her father's Shingon Buddhist family and her mother's Catholic family, and a homestay with a vegan family in Canada helped lead her toward opening an all-vegan restaurant.

A diner praised the vegan kara-age as so convincing they didn't realize it wasn't chicken, in a writeup of the cafe's plant-based comfort food.

chef_bio.background: Effe is the work of chef-owner Toshiyuki Fujimatsu, who was born in Kyoto in 1962. After graduating from the Tsuji Culinary School in Osaka, he trained at a long-established Kyoto Italian restaurant before moving to Italy at age 24. There he cooked at acclaimed kitchens including the two-Michelin-starred Guido and Balzi Rossi, as well as Boccon di Vino, a restaurant tied to the Slow Food movement. He first opened Cucina Naturale Effe in February 2018, then, after deepening his commitment to plant-based cooking and earning a Raw Food Meister certification, reopened in August 2020 as the vegan kitchen known today as Saishoku Ryori Effe, tucked into the Gojo-Karasuma neighborhood of Kyoto.
chef_bio.philosophy: Fujimatsu cooks by a simple credo: today's cooking creates tomorrow's body. Meals, he believes, are central to health and a full daily life, and his vegetable dishes are meant to carry the gentleness of nature's blessings.
chef_bio.specialty: A vegan kitchen built around vegetables, with as many as 30 varieties appearing across a single meal, sourced from trusted farmers and seasoned with house-made touches like salt koji and amazake. Signature plates include the gluten-free rice-flour bread and the enzyme brown rice, cooked with red beans and sea salt and served at its peak texture on the third day. The cooking is free of meat, fish, dairy, eggs, refined white sugar, and wheat flour, with the one exception of an ancient-grain (spelt) pasta.

anecdotes.text: Before opening his own place, Fujimatsu spent his twenties cooking in Italy at two-Michelin-starred kitchens including Guido and Balzi Rossi, and at Boccon di Vino, a restaurant connected to the Slow Food movement.

chef_bio.background: Veg Out sits on the first floor of the cheerful yellow TAMISA building beside the Kamo River, a short walk from Keihan Shichijo Station. The cafe is paired with the TAMISA yoga studio upstairs, and the two were conceived together as one place: somewhere you could move, eat well, and unwind. The founders describe wanting to create a space where you could relax gently, as peacefully as a plant basking in the light. Large windows open onto the river and greenery, flooding the room with natural light, and the whole spot is built around the idea that healthy food and a calm atmosphere belong side by side. A sister location sits near the Nishiki Market in central Kyoto.
chef_bio.philosophy: The team frames veganism not as restriction but as a way of living rooted in gratitude (kansha) for the natural cycles that sustain us. They draw on the spirit of Buddhist shojin (temple) cuisine and its stance of avoiding unnecessary harm, and they care about three connected things: animal welfare, personal health (food free of additives and chemical seasonings), and the environment. Rather than demanding perfection, they encourage eating consciously and plant-based when you can, even if not every day, and they say each dish is prepared with all of their hearts.
chef_bio.specialty: A fully plant-based menu built on naturally farmed, organically grown vegetables (including Kyoto's famous Kyo-yasai) and grains, with no animal products, additives, or artificial seasonings. The house favorite is the Veg Out Plate; other signatures include the Buddha Bowl with homemade falafel that's crispy outside and soft within, served over brown rice with seasonal greens, an obanzai-style vegetable plate, a tempeh sandwich, open sandwiches with vegan taco meat and guacamole, and a tomato-coconut curry. Drinks lean into Bonsoy and oat milk, with natural wine and craft beer in the evenings.

The cafe draws on the spirit of Buddhist shojin cuisine and frames plant-based eating as gratitude for nature's cycles rather than strict abstinence.

chef_bio.background: mumokuteki cafe sits on the upper floor of the mumokuteki goods & wears shop, just off the Teramachi shopping arcade in downtown Kyoto. It is run by the mumokuteki group, which builds everything it does around the idea of 'creating life' — and that idea reaches all the way back to the soil. The group farms its own land at mumokutekifarm in Miyama, in the mountains north of Kyoto, where it grows pesticide-free rice, and sources its vegetables from contracted farmers across the Kinki region who use careful, low-impact methods. That farm-to-table chain is the quiet backbone of the kitchen: the food you eat here started as their rice and their growers' produce.
chef_bio.philosophy: Eat with peace of mind. The kitchen uses absolutely no animal-derived ingredients — no eggs, dairy, refined sugar, meat, fish, or chemical seasonings — so that whether you have allergies, are vegan or vegetarian, or simply care a little about your health, you can enjoy a meal here without hesitation. Even the dashi is plant-based, made from kombu and shiitake rather than animal stock.
chef_bio.specialty: A fully plant-based Japanese menu built so that vegans, vegetarians, and people with allergies can order without second-guessing. The signature is the 'mumokuteki Special Set of 3' — a hamburger built on tofu and okara (soy pulp), okara karaage (fried okara), and rich miso katsu. They are also known for inventive desserts that use no dairy at all: a tiramisu and seasonal cheesecake built on cashews instead of cheese, and a soy-milk soft serve.

anecdotes.text: The group grows its own pesticide-free rice at mumokutekifarm in Miyama, Kyoto, and brings in vegetables from contracted Kinki-region farmers who use safe, low-impact methods.
The miso soup is made entirely from kombu and shiitake dashi, with no animal stock — part of the kitchen's all-vegan, gentle-on-the-body approach.
Desserts reimagine dairy classics without any animal products: a tiramisu and a seasonal cheesecake made with cashews instead of cheese.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: mumokuteki.com and Tabelog confirm an entirely animal-product-free menu (no eggs, dairy, refined sugar, meat, fish or chemical seasonings), kombu-and-shiitake dashi, pesticide-free rice from mumokutekifarm in Miyama (Nantan) and vegetables from contracted Kinki-region farmers, the tofu-hamburger / okara-karaage / miso-katsu set, and cashew-based tiramisu and cheesecake.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The cafe offers some gluten-free menu items (including a Sesame Miso Soy Milk Ramen Set and several desserts marked gluten-free), but states plainly that the kitchen is NOT a dedicated gluten-free kitchen and that utensils and dishes may carry traces of wheat. This means it cannot be considered safe for celiac diners — treat the GF items as lower-gluten, not zero-risk, and confirm directly if you are highly sensitive.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Several dishes use a soy-sauce base (e.g. the fried okara-konjac in the signature set). Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) typically contains wheat, so soy-sauce-seasoned items should be assumed to contain wheat unless staff confirm a wheat-free tamari is used. The existing note that tamari may be available on request points to this being a per-dish, ask-the-staff situation.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Cross-contact risk for vegans is structurally low: the entire kitchen is animal-product-free — no eggs, dairy, meat, or fish are used anywhere — so there are no animal ingredients in the kitchen to cross-contaminate with.
Even the dashi/stock is plant-based (kombu and shiitake), removing the most common hidden-animal pitfall (fish/bonito stock) found in Japanese cooking.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The English menu clearly lists information important to vegans, such as whether fish stock is used, which makes it easier to identify what is safe before ordering.

The cafe explicitly welcomes guests with allergies alongside vegans and vegetarians, framing the whole menu around being able to dine 'with peace of mind' — but for specific allergen questions it is best to confirm with staff, as detailed cross-contamination protocols are not published.

positives.text: 100% vegan kitchen — no animal-derived ingredients of any kind, so animal-product cross-contact is not a concern for vegan diners.
Also avoids eggs, dairy, refined sugar, and chemical seasonings, and uses plant-based kombu/shiitake dashi.
Offers a dedicated set of gluten-free menu items and is upfront about the kitchen not being a dedicated GF environment, which lets sensitive diners make an informed choice.

ChIJLyNa5LcJAWARrcc-BOUsfc8.notes: 7-seat vegan izakaya (Kiyamachi). Soy-meat yakitori/yakiniku, obanzai, dumplings, miso rice balls. Owner cooks solo; queue.

chef_bio.background: Nijiya (虹屋) is a tiny, fully vegan izakaya tucked into Kyoto's Kiyamachi neighbourhood, a short walk from Sanjo Keihan Station. It is run by two women who cook everything themselves in a snug counter space of only about six or seven seats. The intimate, no-reservations setup means you eat almost shoulder-to-shoulder with the cooks, and conversation flows easily across the counter. The kitchen is part of the Vegan Farm project, and the warmth of the two owners, their easy smiles and attentiveness, is the thing guests mention as often as the food.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cooking leans on a wholesome, body-friendly idea of vegan Japanese food: a dashi built from konbu (kelp), dried shiitake, daikon and burdock rather than fish, brown rice grown without pesticides, and gyoza made without alliums so nothing lingers on your breath. The owners pair this with a hands-on, personal hospitality that the small counter makes possible.
chef_bio.specialty: The house specialty is genmai dashi chazuke, a bowl of pesticide-free brown rice over which a deeply savoury, entirely plant-based broth is poured at the table (you are often invited to taste the dashi on its own first). Beyond that, Nijiya reimagines izakaya classics without any animal products: soy-meat yakitori and yakiniku skewers that even meat-eaters say are hard to tell from the real thing, gyoza made deliberately without leek, shallot or garlic, yuzu tofu with yuba, an obanzai assortment of Kyoto small plates, grilled miso rice balls, and a chocolate yokan for dessert.

anecdotes.text: The dashi poured over the brown-rice chazuke is made from konbu (kelp), dried shiitake mushroom, daikon and burdock, and guests are encouraged to taste it on its own before pouring it over the rice.
The gyoza are made without leek, shallot or garlic, so there's no lingering smell on your breath afterwards.
Two women prepare all of the dishes themselves in the tiny seven-seat counter space, serving a set 'nijiya course' alongside a la carte plates.
The soy-meat yakitori and yakiniku skewers are praised as tender and flavourful, with diners noting they were hard to distinguish from meat.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Review sources (visitjapan-vegetarian, herbivoresheaven, itravelforveganfood) confirm Nijiya is a roughly seven-seat counter izakaya near Sanjo/Kiyamachi run by two women and 'produced by Vegan Farm', serving genmai dashi chazuke with kombu/shiitake/daikon/burdock dashi over pesticide-free brown rice, allium-free gyoza, and soy-meat yakitori/yakiniku. A specific opening date is not stated in the sources checked.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a wheat-aware caution, not a celiac-safe rating. The menu includes gyoza (wheat-flour wrappers), soy-meat skewers (commonly seasoned with soy sauce and may be wheat-based), and deep-fried tofu in the obanzai assortment, so wheat and shared frying/cooking surfaces are present. No source documents gluten-free preparation, a dedicated fryer, or celiac protocols. Treat as not celiac-safe unless you confirm specific dishes and handling directly with the cooks.
The obanzai assortment is described as including deep-fried tofu, indicating frying happens in the kitchen; no information confirms whether the fryer is dedicated or gluten-free.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The gyoza are served with house-made soy sauce, and soy-meat skewers are part of the menu. Most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, and no source states this soy sauce or seasoning is wheat-free. Assume it contains gluten unless the cooks confirm otherwise.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Nijiya is a fully vegan kitchen with no animal products on the premises, so the risk of animal-product cross-contact is effectively nil. The dashi is built from konbu, dried shiitake, daikon and burdock rather than fish, so it is plant-based.

staff_allergy_handling.text: A reviewer reported the staff have good English and are very attentive, and will be accommodating with sensitivities such as garlic and spices.
With only the two owner-cooks running a six-to-seven-seat counter, requests can be discussed directly, though the very small kitchen may limit how strictly cross-contamination can be controlled.

positives.text: Entirely vegan menu with a plant-based dashi (konbu, dried shiitake, daikon, burdock) instead of fish stock, so no hidden animal products.
Gyoza are made without leek, shallot or garlic, which helps diners avoiding alliums.
Attentive, English-speaking staff described as accommodating to sensitivities like garlic and spices.

ChIJSaRGStYJAWARvgPDbfi5P0M.notes: All-vegan spot by Kyoto Station (Elite Inn B1F). Vegan 'egg' sandwiches, shojin curry, gimbap, cakes. Reserve at busy times.

chef_bio.background: MERCY Vegan Factory opened its Kyoto Station location in September 2024 as a branch of the all-vegan MERCY Vegan Factory that started in Osaka. Tucked into the basement floor (B1F) of the Elite Inn near Kyoto Station, it brought the brand's playful, comfort-food take on plant-based eating to Kyoto, including a rare-for-Japan early-morning breakfast service alongside dinner.
chef_bio.specialty: The kitchen is known for crowd-pleasing vegan comfort food rather than austere temple fare: a much-loved vegan egg salad sandwich, deep-fried kurumafu (a chewy wheat-gluten mock meat that fans rave about), Korean-style gimbap, hearty curries, and a 'criminally good' matcha pudding. The bakery case rounds it out with chocolate-filled melon pan and cinnamon rolls.

anecdotes.text: Diners single out the vegan egg salad sandwich, with one writing they had 'been craving an egg salad sandwich for years and this was perfect,' and the matcha pudding earning a 'criminally good' verdict.

A visitor notes the Kyoto branch opens early for breakfast, which stands out because 'not many vegan spots open early in Japan,' with house curries, fried kurumafu, melon pan and cinnamon rolls on offer.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog confirms MERCY Vegan Factory Kyoto opened on 2024-09-12 in the B1F of Elite Inn Kyoto Station (Shimogyo-ku, Kamayacho 3, ~716 m from Kyoto Station); HappyCow reviews confirm it is a branch of the Osaka original, note breakfast plus dinner service, and praise the vegan egg-salad sandwich, matcha pudding, fried kurumafu, curries, melon pan and cinnamon rolls.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a wheat-heavy kitchen, so it is not a safe choice for celiac diners. Several signature items are built on wheat gluten or wheat flour: the popular deep-fried kurumafu is a wheat-gluten product (one reviewer describes it as 'a little bit like seitan'), and the bakery (melon pan, cinnamon rolls) and the egg-salad sandwich on white bread are all wheat-based.

gf_cross_contamination.text: With wheat gluten (kurumafu/fu) and breads central to the menu, flour is present throughout the kitchen and airborne/surface cross-contamination is likely. Anyone with celiac disease should confirm directly with staff before ordering.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The menu includes curries, gimbap and other savory Japanese/Korean dishes that typically rely on soy sauce; most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. GF gluten content of the soy seasoning has not been documented, so celiac diners should confirm whether wheat-free tamari is used.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The restaurant is fully vegan, with an entirely plant-based menu and no animal products used on premises, so cross-contact with meat, dairy or egg is not a concern here.

positives.text: Because the entire kitchen is vegan, plant-based diners can order freely across the menu without worrying about animal-product cross-contact.

ChIJ2T2SU0wJAWARoYBoPnI08PQ.notes: Basement vegan cafe near Karasuma-Oike. Big Buddha bowls, slow-cooked vegan burger, hibiscus lemonade. Each dish made to order.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, Japan (founder's culinary outlook shaped by five years in New York)
chef_bio.background: Vegginy is the project of Tomomi Horii, who spent five years living in New York. It was there, surrounded by the city's wildly diverse vegetarian and vegan cooking, that her whole idea of plant-based food shifted: she realized it could be rich, satisfying, and genuinely fun rather than an exercise in going without. She brought that energy home to Kyoto, opening Vegginy in the Gosho-minami area just south of the Imperial Palace, a short walk from Kyoto Shiyakusho-mae station. The space is small and cozy, tucked away with a counter and a couple of tables, and Horii cooks with a New York sensibility translated for a Kyoto audience.
chef_bio.philosophy: Horii's aim is to bring Japan more casual, fun, and delicious vegan food (in her words, '日本にももっと気軽で、楽しくておいしいヴィーガン料理を') - plant-based eating that feels abundant and welcoming rather than restrictive.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegginy is known for its special vegan burger: a spiced chickpea-paste patty bulked out with three kinds of mushroom, grains, and spices for an umami-rich, hearty bite, layered on a soft homemade bun with roasted onions, salted cucumber, and tomato so you get sweetness, salt, and acidity all at once. Beyond the burger, the kitchen turns out colorful, generous plates like a power Buddha bowl and bibimbap, plus weekly-changing vegan specials and homemade baked goods made with coconut oil.

anecdotes.text: Five years in New York transformed Tomomi Horii's view of vegetarian food after she experienced the city's many international plant-based cuisines and found them 'so rich and satisfying' - the inspiration behind Vegginy.

The signature burger's patty is built on a chickpea base mixed with three varieties of mushroom and spices for deep umami, served on a slightly sweet, moist homemade bun with roasted onions and salted cucumber.
Horii applies her New York experience to create weekly-changing vegan menus and homemade baked goods made with coconut oil.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: leafkyoto and life-info confirm owner Tomomi Horii spent five years in New York, where diverse plant-based food reshaped her view of vegan cuisine as 'rich and satisfying', and opened Vegginy in Gosho-minami near Kyoto Shiyakusho-mae; they confirm her quote '日本にももっと気軽で、楽しくておいしいヴィーガン料理を', the chickpea-and-three-mushroom patty on a sweet moist homemade bun with roasted onions and salted cucumber, weekly-changing menus and coconut-oil baked goods.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The signature vegan burger is served on a homemade bun made from wheat flour and whole wheat flour, so the burger as served is not gluten-free. Wheat is baked in-house, which means flour is handled in the kitchen.

Some components are naturally gluten-free in themselves - the patty is chickpea-paste based, and the kitchen also offers salad-style and bowl dishes (Buddha bowl, bibimbap) - but no dedicated gluten-free preparation or cross-contamination controls are documented. Celiac diners should confirm directly with the owner before ordering.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No specific soy sauce or seasoning ingredient details are documented. As is typical in Japan, any soy sauce used likely contains wheat unless confirmed otherwise, so wheat-sensitive and celiac diners should ask about sauces and seasonings.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegginy is a fully vegan kitchen - the entire menu is plant-based with no animal products on premises - so animal cross-contact is not a concern. The bun uses soy milk rather than dairy.
vegan_cross_contact.source_wording: HappyCow category badge: 'Vegan' (all-vegan venue) — 'Restaurant with a selection of sandwiches, burgers, and sweet treats.'

staff_allergy_handling.text: Reviewers describe the staff as very friendly and the owner as passionate about her work and a great English speaker, which should make it easy to ask about ingredients and accommodations. No specific allergy-handling protocol is documented, so discuss your needs directly when ordering.

positives.text: Fully vegan kitchen, so no risk of animal-product cross-contact; the menu is entirely plant-based.
Friendly, English-speaking owner who is hands-on and passionate, making it straightforward to discuss ingredients and dietary needs.
Food is made largely from scratch - homemade buns, patties, and baked goods - so the owner knows the ingredients in each dish.

ChIJGVRVdgAHAWARYgpMlKmu06k.notes: Beloved vegan cafe south of Kyoto Station (Minami). Vegan 'katsu' bowl, veg curry, plum soda, great coffee. Next to a vegan grocer.

chef_bio.background: Hachidori Table (ハチドリTable) is a small plant-based light-meal and coffee shop in Kyoto's Minami-ku, located near Toji Temple (Hachijo-cho 438, about a 14-minute walk from Kyoto Station). Japanese listings describe it as essentially 100% plant-based, using ingredients such as soy meat, and free of the 'five pungent' Buddhist-avoided ingredients (green onion, onion, garlic, Chinese chives and rakkyo), which aligns it with shojin/Buddhist-influenced vegan cooking. The menu is built around easy everyday dishes like curry rice and udon. Daytime hours are about 11:00-15:00 with an evening reservation-only slot (17:00-19:00), closed Mondays; the specific owner/chef is not named in available public sources.
chef_bio.philosophy: Approachable, essentially fully plant-based everyday food that also excludes the five pungent roots, making it suitable for strict vegetarian and Buddhist diners.
chef_bio.specialty: Plant-based comfort dishes such as soy-meat curry rice and udon; coffee.

anecdotes.text: The shop avoids the 'five pungent' ingredients (negi, onion, garlic, nira, rakkyo) in addition to being essentially fully plant-based, using ingredients such as soy meat.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Vegewel and Japan VegeMap describe the Kyoto Hachidori Table as a near-100% plant-based light-meal/coffee shop near Toji (Minami-ku, Hachijo-cho 438), five-pungent-free, using soy meat, serving curry rice and udon; hours ~11:00-15:00 lunch plus reservation-only evenings (17:00-19:00), closed Monday. A separately named 'Hachidori table' in Tottori is a different establishment. No owner name is published, and no source checked confirms an adjacent 'DAICHU' shop.

An English menu is available and the staff are described as welcoming, with dishes made fresh to order.

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, Japan (Higashiyama ward, near Sanjusangendo temple)
chef_bio.background: Shio Veg Cafe was founded by Harsha Sharma, who brings close to a decade of experience in the cafe world to this Kyoto venture. The cafe opened in September 2024 and sits in a wonderfully convenient spot for sightseers: just a few steps from the Sanjusangendo temple and directly across the street from the Kyoto National Museum, in a space that blends an old-Kyoto atmosphere with a bright, modern plant-based kitchen. The aim from the start has been to make vegetarian and vegan food welcoming to everyone, vegetarians and meat-eaters alike, with an emphasis on sustainability and food made from scratch rather than anything pre-packaged.
chef_bio.philosophy: A from-scratch, nothing-artificial approach to plant-based cooking, with a stated emphasis on sustainability, mindful eating, and making vegetarian and vegan food approachable for a wide audience.
chef_bio.specialty: Plant-based cafe fare made fresh in-house. Diners single out the tofu sandwich, the avocado and guacamole toasts (one visitor called it the best they had ever had), and the baked goods, especially the banana walnut and pumpkin nutmeg muffins and chewy cookies. They bake their own bread, including sourdough, and pour matcha lattes and specialty coffee (oat milk available).

anecdotes.text: The cafe sits a few steps from Sanjusangendo temple and directly across from the Kyoto National Museum, blending an old-Kyoto feel with a fresh plant-based menu.

Founder Harsha Sharma launched the cafe in September 2024 after around nine years in the cafe industry, with the goal of introducing vibrant vegetarian and vegan flavours to a broad audience while emphasizing sustainability.
All of the food is made from scratch, with diners praising the freshly made tofu sandwiches, guacamole toast and house-baked muffins and cookies.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a from-scratch bakery-style cafe that bakes its own bread and sourdough on site and serves toasts, muffins and cookies, so wheat flour is heavily present in the kitchen. Celiac diners should treat the cafe as not verified celiac-safe and confirm options directly with staff before ordering.

Dairy is present in the kitchen, so strict vegans should specify a vegan order and confirm there is no cross-contact.
The listing states the cafe offers vegan and egg-free menu options.

positives.text: The cafe has a clearly marked vegan and egg-free menu, and sandwiches including the bread are vegan, with several other items available made vegan on request.
Food is made from scratch with no pre-packaged ingredients, and reviewers consistently praise the freshness of the tofu sandwiches, guacamole toast and baked goods.

chef_bio.background: Cafe Gallery Sun (燦) occupies a kyomachiya, a traditional Kyoto wooden townhouse, that dates back to around 1916, when it was first built as a private home. More than a century later it was taken over by architect Takeshi Yamazaki, who spent about six months redesigning the space alongside his regular work before opening the cafe on 22 October 2022. The result is part cafe, part design studio and part gallery, all under one roof on Gokomachi Street in Shimogyo. One of the most-admired details is the ceiling, finished with an embossed washi (Japanese paper) pattern made by the renowned Kyoto paper house Kyo Karakami Maruni, giving the bright, calm room a distinctly Kyoto craft sensibility.
chef_bio.philosophy: An architect's eye runs through the whole experience, pairing a restored century-old townhouse and handcrafted Kyoto materials with a small, all-vegan menu where, as guests often note, everything is made with a lot of care.
chef_bio.specialty: A fully plant-based menu of unfussy, carefully made dishes. Regulars come for the avocado sandwich, the open-faced avocado sandwich, the ham-and-vegetable sandwich and the pasta of the day served with a baguette and salad. The bread comes from Slō, a much-loved Kyoto bakery. Sweets round things out, with carrot, banana and chocolate cakes, plus vanilla and rum-raisin ice cream.

anecdotes.text: The cafe lives inside a roughly 107-year-old kyomachiya built in 1916, which architect Takeshi Yamazaki redesigned over about six months and opened as Cafe Gallery Sun on 22 October 2022.

The ceiling is a signature feature, finished with an embossed washi pattern made by Kyoto paper company Kyo Karakami Maruni, and the bread served with the sandwiches and pasta comes from the popular Kyoto bakery Slō.
The space doubles as the architect's design studio and a small gallery, and visitors describe a calm, bright, stylish room where the all-vegan menu is small but everything is made with great care.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free menu or cross-contamination protocol is documented in available sources. This cafe should not be considered celiac-safe; a celiac diner would need to confirm directly with the staff before eating.

chef_bio.background: Smoothie etc lives on the second floor of the TAMISA yoga studio in the Sanjo-Teramachi neighbourhood, a calm pocket tucked above one of central Kyoto's busiest shopping streets. The cafe began as a way to nourish the studio's yoga students from the inside out, offering food and drink meant to be kind to both mind and body rather than relying on artificial products. It later widened its doors to travellers and neighbours looking for honest, plant-based fare. In August 2018 it was reborn from the earlier Cosy Cafe under the name Smoothie etc, built around the idea of being 'Mindful and Convenient': conscious daily choices that are still easy to fold into real life. Regulars affectionately shorten the name to 'Sumueto.'
chef_bio.philosophy: Food and drink should be 'Mindful and Convenient' - kind to body and mind, made from additive-free, plant-based, organic and fair-trade ingredients, and easy to bring into everyday life.
chef_bio.specialty: Smoothies built on organically grown and pesticide-free (or reduced-pesticide) fruit and vegetables sourced from around Kyoto, each laced with ginger and warming spices meant to aid digestion. Signatures include Super Green, Beet Ginger, Spice Nut Milk, and the Cacao Energy smoothie made with banana, amazake, cacao and soy milk. The smoothie bowl, topped with banana, berries, house-made granola and nuts, has become a draw, alongside gluten-free rice-flour muffins sweetened with brown sugar, maple syrup, dried fruit and nuts instead of refined white sugar.

anecdotes.text: The cafe grew out of TAMISA yoga studio as a way to support yoga students from a dietary perspective, before expanding to welcome travellers and other visitors seeking accessible vegan food and drink.
Formerly known as Cosy Cafe, it was rebranded in August 2018 as Smoothie etc around the concept 'Mindful + Convenient.'

Smoothies use organically grown, pesticide-free or reduced-pesticide produce from around Kyoto, with ginger and spices added to aid digestion, and rice-flour muffins are sweetened with brown sugar, maple syrup, dried fruit and nuts rather than white sugar.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The cafe is fully plant-based and offers a number of gluten-free items, including smoothie bowls, rice-flour muffins, cakes and cookies. No information on shared prep surfaces or flour-dust cross-contamination is published, so a strict celiac should confirm preparation directly with staff before ordering.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: This is a smoothie- and baked-goods-focused vegan cafe rather than a savory soy-sauce kitchen; documented menus emphasize fruit, vegetable and spice smoothies, soups, vegan bread and rice-flour baked goods. No specific soy-sauce details are published. Soy milk and amazake do appear in several smoothies, which is relevant for soy-sensitive diners.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is described as 100 percent vegan and plant-based, with all items additive-free, so animal-product cross-contact risk is low.

staff_allergy_handling.text: A diner with a nut allergy reported a serious incident: a smoothie bowl arrived garnished with visible walnuts, and after sending it back, staff offered only to scoop the nuts out rather than remake the dish, assuring him it was 'just the garnish.' chef_bio.background: Padma is the work of Hisano Kuno, who came to plant-based cooking through a deep interest in Buddhism and yoga. Years ago she traveled to India, where alongside her spiritual practice she learned to cook with spices and to prepare vegetarian food. Back in Japan she studied macrobiotics and Buddhist temple cuisine (shojin ryori), but found that a rigid macrobiotic approach didn't suit her own body, so she gradually shaped a gentler, more personal style of cooking. Drawn by Kyoto's people, its young, conscientious farmers, and the quality of its vegetables, she left Tokyo and settled in the city, opening Padma with the help of friends who helped renovate the space. The name Padma means lotus flower, an Eastern symbol of purity and awakening, and the room carries a warm, lived-in atmosphere that blends Japanese and early-20th-century Western touches.
chef_bio.philosophy: Kuno calls her food 'heiwateki gohan' - peaceful meals: dishes that everyone can enjoy regardless of dietary needs, without animal products, made so simply that a guest who asks how something is cooked can actually understand the answer. She leans on fermented seasonings - miso, plum vinegar and sesame paste - as her three pillars for depth, prioritizes organic and pesticide-free Kyoto vegetables and brown rice, and aims to cook gentle, healing food adapted to the person in front of her.
chef_bio.specialty: A fully plant-based, Kyoto-vegetable-centered table built around Kuno's 'Peaceful Meal Plate' - a generous seasonal spread of many small vegetable dishes. Signature items include a tempeh cutlet/croquette and a katsudon made with kuruma-fu (wheat gluten) standing in for meat, plus Indian-influenced spice cooking. A point of pride is the handcrafted RUSTO tempeh, made in Shiga from soybeans and natural groundwater with no preservatives, by an Indonesian maker who built his own well and workshop.

anecdotes.text: Kuno's path to the kitchen began with Buddhism and yoga: a trip to India years ago, where she learned both spiritual practice and how to cook vegetarian food with spices.

She studied macrobiotics but found a strict version didn't agree with her own body - root vegetables bothered her pancreas - so she built her own gentler 'peaceful meals' style instead of following any single doctrine.

She moved from Tokyo to Kyoto after being won over by the city's young farmers and the quality of its vegetables, saying Kyoto vegetables are abundant and delicious and that the soil's energy feels like it circulates naturally.
A signature ingredient is RUSTO tempeh, hand-made in Shiga from soybeans and natural groundwater with no preservatives, by an Indonesian maker who dug his own well and built his own workshop.

The menu also includes fried, battered items such as tempura broccoli and a vegetable cutlet, which typically use wheat flour batter and a shared fryer - an additional gluten cross-contact risk.

The founding vision is 'food barrier-free' dining: a place where vegans, people with allergies, the health-conscious, and people from every dietary background can all sit at the same table and eat with peace of mind. The dining room is built around natural materials with a modern Japanese feel, garden views, and a mix of counter seats, tables, and a private space.
